content: The Cuban government operates a national health system, taking full fiscal and administrative responsibility for the healthcare of its citizens. Private hospitals and clinics are not permitted. The current Minister of Public Health is José Ramón Balaguer. Before the Spanish conquest, indigenous Cuban societies practiced traditional medicine, with high-status practitioners known as Bohiques. After colonization, Cuban medicine adopted Spanish traditions influenced by Moorish, Greek, and Roman practices. Chinese medicine also became part of Cuban healthcare, with figures like 19th-century doctor Cham Bom Biam, known as El Medico Chino, gaining prominence. Modern Western medicine has been practiced in Cuba since at least the early 19th century, with the first surgical clinic established in 1823. Notable Cuban doctors include Carlos Finlay, who discovered how yellow fever spreads, working alongside Walter Reed, James Carroll, and Aristides Agramonte. During the U.S. occupation (1898–1902), yellow fever was nearly eradicated due to efforts by Clara Maass and Jesse W. Lazear. By the 1950s, Cuba had some of the best health indices in the Americas, with life expectancy and doctor-to-population ratios surpassing many European countries. However, healthcare access was unequal, with only 8% of the rural population receiving care. After the Cuban Revolution, the government prioritized universal healthcare. In 1960, Che Guevara outlined goals for public health, emphasizing preventive medicine and public hygiene. Despite these ambitions, nearly half of Cuba's physicians emigrated to the U.S., leaving only 3,000 doctors in the country. The Ministry of Public Health began nationalizing and regionalizing medical services in 1960. In 1976, Article 50 of the Cuban Constitution guaranteed free healthcare, including medical and dental care, vaccinations, and disease prevention programs. Cuba's doctor-to-patient ratio improved dramatically, from 9.2 doctors per 10,000 people in 1958 to 58.2 per 10,000 in 1999. Universal vaccination programs in the 1960s eradicated diseases like polio and rubella, though economic hardships in the 1990s led to a resurgence of diseases like tuberculosis and hepatitis. Maternal and prenatal care programs reduced infant mortality rates. By 2007, Cuba had computerized national networks for blood banks, nephrology, and medical imaging, aiming to maintain free, high-quality healthcare and foster research and expert collaboration. Cuba's healthcare system has faced material shortages due to the U.S. embargo and the loss of Soviet subsidies. Despite this, the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that Cuba's infant mortality rate is lower than that of the U.S., with 5 deaths per 1,000 live births compared to 7 in the U.S. Life expectancy in Cuba is comparable to the U.S., with males living to 75 years and females to 79 years. Cuba has nearly twice as many physicians per capita as the U.S. High abortion rates, particularly in the 1980s, have contributed to low infant mortality rates. Among adults under 49, accidents are the leading cause of death, while heart disease and cancer predominate among older adults. Suicide rates in Cuba are among the highest in Latin America, at 18.2 per 100,000 people. Cuba has a low HIV/AIDS prevalence, with only 0.1% of the population affected, one of the lowest rates in the world. In the 1980s, Cuba implemented compulsory HIV testing and isolated those who tested positive, a policy later discontinued. Since 1996, Cuba has produced generic antiretroviral drugs, significantly reducing treatment costs. Education on HIV/AIDS is provided by the Cuban National Center for Sex Education. However, new HIV infections are rising due to income inequality and a growing sex industry. Cuba's mother-to-child transmission prevention program remains effective, with all pregnant women tested for HIV and treated if necessary. The U.S. embargo has severely impacted Cuba's access to medicines and medical supplies. The Cuban Democracy Act of 1992 prohibited U.S. subsidiaries from trading with Cuba, increasing costs and limiting access to essential medical items. Although the U.S. has approved some licenses for medical sales to Cuba, restrictions and logistical challenges make imports difficult. Cuba also faces financial constraints, lacking access to international credit and hard currency. The collapse of the Soviet Union further strained resources, forcing Cuba to rely on alternative and herbal medicine. Cuba has one of the highest doctor-to-patient ratios globally, with one doctor for every 170 residents. All healthcare professionals work for the state, and private practice is prohibited. However, low salaries—around $15–20 per month—have led some doctors to seek higher-paying jobs in the tourism industry. Economic hardships have also fueled a black market for healthcare, where patients pay under the table for faster or better services. Cuba has a strong international healthcare presence, with agreements with UN agencies like WHO and UNICEF. Cuban doctors serve in 68 countries, including Venezuela, where they exchange medical services for subsidized oil. Programs like Operación Milagro provide free eye surgeries to Latin Americans, funded by the Venezuelan government. Cuba also treats children affected by the Chernobyl disaster and has sent medical teams to disaster-stricken areas worldwide. Cuba attracts around 20,000 health tourists annually, generating $40 million in revenue. Foreign patients seek treatments for conditions like neurological disorders, retinitis pigmentosa, and orthopedic issues. Cuba also exports medical products, including vaccines and alternative medicines like policosanol (PPG) for cholesterol reduction. Cuba integrates alternative medicine into its healthcare system, using techniques like acupuncture, homeopathy, and herbal remedies. Children learn about medicinal plants in school, and the government promotes natural products like Vimang®, derived from mango tree bark. Cuba's medical research is government-funded, with limited private investment. Notable achievements include a study on inactivated poliovirus vaccine, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, which demonstrated its effectiveness in tropical conditions. Cuba has been polio-free since 1963 but continues mass immunization campaigns. Cuba's healthcare system has received international praise for its focus on prevention and community-based care. Organizations like the UN and the World Bank have lauded its achievements despite economic challenges. However, critics highlight issues like low doctor salaries, outdated facilities, and shortages of essential drugs. Some accuse the government of prioritizing foreign patients and senior officials over ordinary Cubans, creating disparities in care quality. The U.S. State Department and other sources argue that Cuba's pre-revolutionary healthcare system was already advanced, with high physician-to-population ratios and low infant mortality rates.
